newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Meadowbrook takes corrective action.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Meadowbrook takes corrective action.

text.p: Meadowbrook Insurance Group Inc, which reported an unexpected 1996 third-quarter earnings shortfall because of unprofitable surety business, said Wednesday it has taken corrective action.
Jon Sasinowski, executive vice president, investor relations, said the company fired some general agents who failed to follow company underwriting standards.
"We're not writing any new business with those agents," Sasinowski told Reuters in a telephone interview.

Meadowbrook posted earnings of $492,000 or $0.05 per share for the quarter compared with $2.8 million or $0.41 per share a year ago. "The street was expecting profit of $3.6 million," Sasinowski said.

Higher than expected losses in a discontinued portion of the surety bond business (performance bonds for small to medium size contractors) resulted in a $2.9 million shortfall and another $200,000 was related to lower investment income.
"Now we have to prove to the market we can meet our growth expectations, and we fully intend to do so," Sasinowski said.

He said Meadowbrook's goal was to average 25 percent growth a year. "Our present backlog of business going into the fourth quarter and into 1997 leads us to believe we will fully meet our revenue and profit growth expectations in 1997."
Shares of the Southfield, Mich.-based alternative risk management company closed Wednesday 10-3/4 at 15-5/8, a 41 percent drop.
Sasinowski said its other businesses were operating "more profitably than expected. This (situation) overshadows the success of everything else."
Dean Witter analyst Michael Lewis said he reduced his earnings estimates on Meadowbrook to $1 from $1.54 for the current year and to $1.70 from $1.90 for next year.

"We were going to go to a neutral rating, but after a 40 percent-plus selloff, we decided to stay at a buy," said Lewis, adding that in his view "the market reaction was overdone. We still think the company is a decent alternative play, growing at 20 percent a year."
